title: BMM Developer Notes
text:
Overview
Last update: 16.10.2026
These notes are for developers who want to add a model to bmm. They explain how the package is put together and walk through the steps of contributing a model, from setting up your system to opening the pull request.
bmm covers five kinds of tasks: continuous reproduction (mixture models, IMM, SDM), categorical recall and n-AFC decisions (M3), processing-tree models (MPT), detection, recognition and confidence judgments (the signal detection models), and choices with response times (DDM, EZDM, Censored-Shifted Wald). bmm_models() lists them. The package requires R >= 4.1.0 and uses the native pipe |> throughout.
This guide describes bmm at the v1.4.1 tag. Anything merged after that tag may not be reflected here yet. If you run into problems, open an issue on GitHub.

title: BMM Developer Notes
text:
From idea to merged model

Open an issue with the new_model template and agree with the maintainers on the model and the release it targets.
Fork bmm, set up your system and create a branch named after the issue (1  System setup).
Generate the model file with use_model_template() and fill it in (5  Adding a new model). Write the distribution functions first and the prediction functions after.
Add the model’s tests and its test cases, and run document(), test() and check().
Run a parameter recovery study, and add an example dataset, an article and a NEWS bullet.
Open the pull request against the branch you started from and fill in the template (5  Adding a new model has the checklist).

title: BMM Developer Notes
text:
How to read these notes

System setup and Git workflow get you a working fork.
Code structure explains what happens when a user calls bmm(), and Example models shows two real model files.
Adding a new model is the step-by-step guide, ending with a checklist for the pull request.
Coding conventions lists what review will check your code against.

The appendix, Reference, collects details you need only when you hit a particular problem, such as within-chain threading or a parameter name that collides with brms.

title: BMM Developer Notes
text:
The rules for contributing
Which branch to target, what a pull request must contain, how many reviews it needs and how model fits for articles are handled are set out in bmm’s CONTRIBUTING.md. These notes do not repeat those rules. For a new model, two things matter from the start:

Open an issue with the new_model template first, so that you agree with the maintainers that the model fits the package and in which release it will appear.
Make the model easy to check. The reviewer reads your likelihood against its published source and looks at your parameter recovery. Include a short, runnable example with a small simulated dataset, and say in the pull request how long it takes to fit and what output to expect.

title: 1  System setup
text: 1.1 Setting up a local fork of the bmm repository

title: 1  System setup
text:
Fork the bmm GitHub repository. This creates a copy of the repository in your own GitHub account.

Clone your fork to your local machine, and add the main repository as a remote so that you can keep your branch up to date: git remote add upstream https://github.com/popov-lab/bmm.git.
Create a branch for your model. Branch from develop, or, if the issue for your model is planned for a later release, from that release’s integration branch (dev-x.y.0); the issue’s milestone tells you which. Name the branch after the issue, as <issue-number>-short-description (for example 349-lba-model), so that branch, issue and pull request are easy to line up.

title: 1  System setup
text:
1.2 Prerequisites
The bmm package requires R >= 4.1.0 (for the native pipe |>). It works with both the rstan and the cmdstanr backend. We recommend cmdstanr, which compiles faster and gives better error messages, and the tests that compile Stan code need it:
install.packages("cmdstanr", repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()
Once bmm is loaded (with load_all(), below), bmm_setup() checks the C++ toolchain, cmdstanr with CmdStan, rstan, and the backend bmm() will use. It then compiles and samples a small test model and suggests a fix for every check that failed. Run it before your first fit.

title: 1  System setup
text:
1.3 Package development with devtools
Development runs on the devtools package, whichever editor you work in. The repository ships a bmm.Rproj file, so opening it in RStudio or Positron starts a session in the package root; in any other editor, start R in the repository directory. R Packages is the standard tutorial. The steps you will repeat:

Install the development tools and bmm’s dependencies once:
install.packages(c("devtools", "roxygen2", "testthat", "knitr"))
library(devtools)
install_dev_deps()
Load the package from your local files whenever you change the code:
load_all()  # ctrl+shift+L in RStudio
Do not call library(bmm) or source the files, as that loads the installed version, not the one you are working on.
Before you open a pull request, regenerate the documentation, run the tests and check the package, in this order:
document()  # regenerates man/ and NAMESPACE; never edit those by hand
test()
check()     # 0 errors, 0 warnings; explain any note in the pull request

title: 1  System setup
text:
1.4 Running the tests
test() runs tests/testthat/ in parallel. Two kinds of test there skip themselves when your machine cannot run them:

Tests that compile Stan code need CmdStan. Set BMM_TEST_STAN=false in your environment to skip them deliberately.
Tests that read a stored fit need tests/testthat/assets/, which is left out of the built package, so they skip inside check().

Tests that actually sample live in tests/local/ and never run in test() or check(). They are not required for a pull request, because a weekly CI job runs them, but you can run them with Rscript tests/local/run.R. Run test(reporter = "slow") before a pull request as well: the suite has a time budget that CI enforces, and this reporter shows which of your tests are slow. Chapter 5 says which tests a new model needs.

title: 1  System setup
text:
1.5 Untracked scratch work
Development produces files that belong on your machine rather than in the package: exploratory scripts, fitted model objects, scratch data. bmm’s .gitignore excludes a local/ folder at the root of the repository for this purpose, so anything you put there stays out of your commits. (tests/local/ is a different folder and is tracked.) Your parameter recovery script can live there, but the reviewer has to see its results; Chapter 5 says how.

title: 2  Git and GitHub workflow
text:
2.1 Branches
This chapter is a short summary of the commands you need, not a guide to git.
bmm follows a git-flow model. master holds the latest release and develop the next one. Features planned for a later release collect on integration branches named after that release (dev-x.y.0), which are merged into develop when their release opens. You branch from one of develop or dev-x.y.0 (see Chapter 1) and open your pull request against the same branch.

title: 2  Git and GitHub workflow
text:
2.2 Git commands
Add your changes, commit them and push them to your fork, from any terminal with the repository as the working directory.
Stage specific files rather than everything with git add ., which can pick up files you did not mean to commit, such as fitted model objects:
git add R/model_my_model.R inst/stan_chunks/my_model_functions.stan
git commit -m "A short message describing the change"
git push
Repeat as often as you like before opening the pull request. Small, self-contained commits are easier to review.
Do not commit fitted models. A CI check fails the pull request if any of its commits adds a file over 1 MiB, even if a later commit removes it again; CONTRIBUTING.md says how fits for articles are handled instead.

title: 2  Git and GitHub workflow
text:
2.3 Pull requests
Open the pull request from your fork on GitHub, against the branch you started from. The pull request template asks for what the reviewer needs, with an extra checklist for a new model; fill it in. Review tiers, the recovery evidence a new model needs, and the policy on AI-assisted contributions are in CONTRIBUTING.md.
If you use AI tools, read Chapter 6 before you open the pull request. The ways code generated by a language model typically departs from bmm’s style are the ones that chapter lists: validation in internal helpers, base stop() and sprintf(), a final return(), comments that restate the code, and a recovery study that simulates and fits with the same function.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.1 What happens when a user calls bmm()
You do not have to edit any of the files described here to add a model: use_model_template() (Chapter 5) writes a model file, and the package finds it. This chapter explains what happens to that file when a user fits a model, so that you know which part of it runs when.
bmm() in R/bmm.R knows nothing about specific models. It passes the user’s formula, data and model to a pipeline of S3 generics, and each model supplies methods for the steps where it differs from the default:
configure_fit() holds the whole configuration sequence:
The same function serves stancode(), standata() and default_prior(), which stop early through until. So the methods you write for check_data() and configure_model() are also what a user sees when they inspect the Stan code or the default priors of your model without fitting it.
Three details of bmm() itself concern model authors:

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
bmm(formula, data, model)
|- configure_fit()              R/helpers-model.R
|   |- check_model()            is the model valid, are the user's links allowed
|   |- check_data()             validate and transform the data     <- model method
|   |- check_formula()          one formula per parameter
|   |- configure_model()        brms formula, family, Stan code     <- model method
|   |- configure_prior()        default priors + the user's prior
|   `- create_initfun()         initial values for the sampler
|- brms::brm()                  compile and sample
`- postprocess_brm()            rename, store metadata              <- optional model method



R/helpers-model.R

configure_fit.bmmformula <- function(formula, data = NULL, model = NULL, prior = NULL,
                                     until = "init", frame_args = list()) {
  user_formula <- formula
  # the user's expression for the data lives in the caller of the generic
  # (bmm() or an extractor). It is set before check_data(), whose methods print
  # it (order_data_query()), and again after, because some methods rebuild the
  # data frame without it
  data_name <- substitute_name(data, envir = parent.frame())
  if (!missing(data) && !is.null(data) && (is.list(data) || is.atomic(data))) {
    attr(data, "data_name") <- data_name
  }
  model <- check_model(model, data, formula)
  data <- check_data(model, data, formula)
  attr(data, "data_name") <- data_name
  formula <- check_formula(model, data, formula)
  config_args <- configure_model(model, data, formula)
  if (until == "model") {
    return(nlist(config_args, model, user_formula))
  }
  prior <- brms::do_call(
    configure_prior, c(list(model, data, config_args$formula, prior), frame_args)
  )
  # the prior decides which parameters exist, so the inits are built from it
  if (until == "init") {
    config_args$init <- brms::do_call(
      create_initfun, c(list(model, data, config_args$formula, prior), frame_args)
    )
  }
  nlist(config_args, prior, model, user_formula)
}




Caching. With file_refit = "on_change", a cached fit is reused only if the Stan code and data are unchanged. configure_model() must therefore generate the same Stan code for the same inputs.
Model-frame arguments. brms_frame_args() picks out the brm() arguments that change the model frame (data2, knots, drop_unused_levels) and passes them to configure_prior() and create_initfun(). This is why those methods need ... in their signature.
Threading. local_brms_threads() records whether the user asked for within-chain threading, because a model may need to generate different Stan code for it (Section A.5).

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.2 The bmmformula class
Users specify what to estimate with a bmmformula (alias bmf()): a list of formulas, one per model parameter. Unlike a brmsformula, it has no response variable on the left-hand side, because the response is named when the model object is constructed.
f <- bmf(kappa ~ 0 + set_size + (1 | id), c ~ 1 + (1 | id), a ~ 1)
f <- bmf(kappa ~ condition, a = 0.5)  # '=' fixes 'a' to 0.5 instead of estimating it
A parameter the user does not mention gets an intercept-only formula, with a message. During configuration, the bmf2bf() method converts the bmmformula to a brmsformula. It adds the response as the first formula line and turns each parameter formula into a linear (brms::lf()) or non-linear (brms::nlf()) component.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.3 Models
Each model is an S3 class with an internal constructor, .model_<name>(), and a user-facing alias, <name>(). The parameters, links, fixed parameters, priors and initialization ranges live in a separate list, .<name>_defaults, or, for a model with several versions, .<name>_version_table (Section A.6). The constructor reads its fields from that list:
.my_model_defaults <- list(
  parameters = list(
    par1 = "Parameter 1 = description of parameter 1",
    par2 = "Parameter 2 = description of parameter 2"
  ),
  links = list(par1 = "identity", par2 = "log"),
  fixed_parameters = list(mu = 0),
  priors = list(
    par1 = list(main = "normal(0, 1)", effects = "normal(0, 0.5)", sd = "exponential(1)"),
    par2 = list(main = "normal(0, 0.5)", effects = "normal(0, 0.5)", sd = "exponential(2)")
  ),
  init_ranges = list(par1 = c(-1, 1), par2 = c(0.5, 1.5))
)

.model_my_model <- function(resp_var1 = NULL, required_arg1 = NULL,
                            links = NULL, call = NULL, ...) {
  out <- structure(
    list(
      resp_vars = nlist(resp_var1),
      other_vars = nlist(required_arg1),
      domain = "",
      task = "",
      name = "",
      citation = character(),
      version = "NA",
      requirements = "",
      parameters = .my_model_defaults[["parameters"]],
      links = .my_model_defaults[["links"]],
      fixed_parameters = .my_model_defaults[["fixed_parameters"]],
      default_priors = .my_model_defaults[["priors"]],
      init_ranges = .my_model_defaults[["init_ranges"]]
    ),
    class = c("bmmodel", "my_model"),
    call = call
  )
  set_links(out, links)
}
The fields of the specification:

parameters: the parameters a user can estimate or fix, each with a description. A dummy parameter that exists only for brms stays out (Section A.2).
links: the link function of each parameter, which maps the scale Stan samples on to the scale the parameter is interpreted on. Users can change links through the alias’s links argument; set_links() validates their choice (Section A.1).
fixed_parameters: parameters held at a constant, such as list(mu = 0).
priors: per parameter, a prior for the intercept (main), for regression coefficients (effects) and for random-effect standard deviations (sd); see Section 3.8.
init_ranges: optional c(lower, upper) windows for initial values, for parameters whose likelihood is undefined in part of their range (Section A.3).

The metadata fields (domain, task, name, citation, requirements) fill the help page and the model listings. domain decides under which task group bmm_models() and the website list the model, so reuse the string of the models yours belongs with. Tests check that every constructor runs with no arguments and lists its fields in the order above.
The alias validates the user’s arguments and calls the constructor. Its help page is generated from the constructor’s fields by model_docs():
#' @title `r .model_my_model()$name`
#' @name my_model
#' @details `r model_docs(.model_my_model())`
#' @param resp_var1 A description of the response variable
#' @param required_arg1 A description of the required argument
#' @param ... used internally for testing, ignore it
#' @return An object of class `bmmodel`
#' @keywords bmmodel
#' @export
my_model <- function(resp_var1, required_arg1, links = NULL, ...) {
  call <- match.call()
  stop_missing_args()
  .model_my_model(resp_var1 = resp_var1, required_arg1 = required_arg1,
                  links = links, call = call, ...)
}
A model with versions adds version = c("v1", "v2") to the alias, validates it with match.arg() and appends the version to the class. use_model_template() generates either variant.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.4 Class chains
The class vector of a model encodes where it sits in the taxonomy, and it decides which methods run:
class = c("bmmodel", <shared class>, <model>, <version>)







Task group
Models and class chains




Continuous reproduction
mixture2p: c("bmmodel", "circular", "mixture2p"); mixture3p: c("bmmodel", "circular", "non_targets", "mixture3p"); imm: c("bmmodel", "circular", "non_targets", "imm", "imm_full"); sdm: c("bmmodel", "circular", "sdm", "sdm_simple")


Categorical recall
m3: c("bmmodel", "m3", "m3_ss")


Processing trees
mpt: c("bmmodel", "mpt")


Signal detection
sdt_yn: c("bmmodel", "sdt", "sdt_yn"), likewise sdt_mafc, sdt_ranking, sdt_cdp; sdt_rating: c("bmmodel", "sdt", "sdt_rating", "sdt_rating_standard")


Choices and response times
ddm: c("bmmodel", "ddm"); ezdm: c("bmmodel", "ezdm", "ezdm_3par"); cswald: c("bmmodel", "cswald", "cswald_simple")



Shared classes such as "circular", "non_targets" and "sdt" carry methods that several models use: check_data.circular() checks that responses are in radians, and check_formula.sdt() refuses the stimulus column as a predictor. Dispatch walks the class vector from left to right, so check_data.bmmodel() runs first and each method hands on to the next with NextMethod(). The model’s own method runs last. Chapter 4 follows one such chain through the IMM.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.5 S3 generics
Each pipeline step is a generic, such as


R/helpers-model.R

configure_model <- function(model, data, formula) {
   UseMethod('configure_model')
}

and a model adds a method for it, configure_model.my_model(). That is how new models are added without editing bmm(). The generics of the pipeline:








Generic
Signature
Defined in




check_model
(model, data = NULL, formula = NULL)
helpers-model.R


check_data
(model, data, formula)
helpers-data.R


check_formula
(model, data, formula)
bmmformula.R


bmf2bf
(model, formula)
bmmformula.R


configure_model
(model, data, formula)
helpers-model.R


configure_prior
(model, data, formula, user_prior, ...)
helpers-prior.R


create_initfun
(model, data, formula, prior = NULL, ...)
helpers-inits.R


postprocess_brm
(model, fit, ...)
helpers-postprocess.R



Match these signatures exactly, including ... and the = NULL defaults. R CMD check compares every method with its generic.
A model writes check_data() and configure_model() methods almost always, bmf2bf() when its response needs wrapping (DDM: rt | dec(response) ~ 1) or packs several columns (vreal(), vint(), trials()), and postprocess_brm() rarely. configure_model() returns nlist(formula, data, stanvars): the brmsformula with its family set, the data, and the Stan code for a custom family. A model built on a native brms family, such as brms::mixture() for the IMM, needs no stanvars.
Further generics let a model adjust behaviour around the pipeline. Each has a default that covers most models; Chapter 5 says when to write a method:

before and after the fit: revert_check_data() (Section 3.7), settable_links() (Section A.1), data_check_findings();
for post-processing: native_transform(), pp_observables() and pp_simulate().

A few more exist for single model families, such as generated_parameters() for MPT or summary_notes() for the SDT models. Their source files explain them.

title: 3  BMM code structure
section: 3.6 Passing information from check_data() to configure_model()
text:
3.6 Passing information from check_data() to configure_model()
check_data() and configure_model() are separate methods and cannot share local variables. When check_data() computes something that configure_model() needs, it stores it as an attribute of the data frame:
# in check_data.non_targets() (R/helpers-data.R)
attr(data, "max_set_size") <- max_set_size
attr(data, "lure_idx_vars") <- lure_idx_vars

# later, in configure_model.imm_full() (R/model_imm.R)
max_set_size <- attr(data, "max_set_size")
lure_idx <- attr(data, "lure_idx_vars")
Two cautions. The infrastructure uses the same channel for its own bookkeeping (check_data.bmmodel() sets data_name and checked), so not every attribute you find is yours. And a configure_model() method can be called directly, without check_data(), so the attribute may be missing. configure_model.sdm() recomputes the value in that case; if you do not guard, make the failure loud.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.7 Re-running check_data() in update()
update(fit) without new data refits on the data stored in the fit. That is brms’s model frame, which holds only the variables the formula uses and is already the output of your check_data(). Running check_data() on it again fails for any model whose check adds, renames or packs columns.
So update() first calls revert_check_data(model, data) to bring the stored frame back into the shape the user’s data had. The default returns the data unchanged, which is right for a check_data() that only validates. If yours changes columns, write a method in R/update.R:

End with NextMethod("revert_check_data"), so that a method on a shared class still runs.
A column your check_data() needs may be missing from the stored frame, because brms keeps only the columns the formula uses. A method that has to rebuild such a column names it in the "rebuilt" attribute of the data, and update() drops it again after the check. Append to that attribute rather than overwriting it.

revert_check_data.m3() and the SDT methods are the examples. The stored_frame case your model registers for the tests (Chapter 5) is what checks that this works.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.8 Default priors
configure_prior() reads each parameter’s entry in priors:

main applies to the intercept. If the user drops the intercept (kappa ~ 0 + condition), it applies to each level of the factor instead. Keep it first in the list: without an intercept, it is found by position.
effects applies to regression coefficients. Without it, brms’ defaults apply.
sd applies to the random-effect standard deviations. Without it, brms falls back to student_t(3, 0, 2.5), which on a log link lets individual values vary by a factor of 12 around the group value. The shipped models use exponential() with a rate chosen by what the parameter measures (Section A.7).

The strings use the format of brms::set_prior(). Correlations among random effects get lkj(2) without anything in the model definition. For a parameter in both fixed_parameters and parameters, such as mu1 in the IMM, the fixed value holds unless the user gives it a formula.

title: 3  BMM code structure
text:
3.9 File organization







File
Contents




R/bmm.R
bmm(). You do not edit it for a new model.


R/helpers-model.R
configure_fit(), check_model(), configure_model() defaults, use_model_template(), and the central tables a new model adds to: data_column_roles, response_annotations()


R/helpers-data.R, -prior.R, -inits.R, -postprocess.R, -parameters.R
The defaults of the other pipeline steps; also the RT data utilities (flag_contaminant_rts(), ezdm_summary_stats())


R/bmmformula.R
bmmformula()/bmf(), check_formula(), bmf2bf()


R/model_<name>.R
One model: specification, constructor, alias, its methods, and the log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred functions of a custom family. MPT, the largest model, is split over several model_mpt_*.R files.


R/helpers-sdt.R, R/helpers-analysis.R
Code shared by the signal detection models, and their ROC/AUC analyses


R/distributions.R
The d*, r* (and where available p*, q*) functions of each model


R/update.R, R/restructure.R
update() with the revert_check_data() methods; bringing old fits up to date


R/data_check.R, R/bmm_setup.R
bmm_data_check() and bmm_setup()


post-processing files
conditional_effects.R, emmeans.R, pp_check.R, pp_observables.R, ppp.R, summary.R, plot.R, report-extract.R. They work on any fitted model.


R/brms-misc.R
A read-only copy of brms internals. Do not edit it.


inst/stan_chunks/
Stan code for custom families, named <model>_<block>.stan; code shared by several models gets its own file (sdt_dist_funs.stan)



Good model files to read first are R/model_ddm.R (flat specification), R/model_cswald.R (version table) and R/model_sdt_yn.R (aggregated counts).
When you write Stan code, remember that the sampler needs continuous gradients. Non-differentiable operations such as fabs() or fmax() cause divergent transitions; where they are mathematically needed, use a smooth stand-in such as sqrt(x^2 + epsilon) for |x|.

title: 4  Example models
text:
4.1 The Interference Measurement Model (IMM)
This chapter walks through two model files in the package. The IMM is built on a native brms family, brms::mixture(), and needs no Stan code of its own; it shows shared classes, check_data() dispatch and non-linear formulas. The DDM is a custom family with its own Stan code; it shows a flat specification, a model without a location parameter, and a custom first formula line. Between them they cover what use_model_template() asks you to fill in.
The IMM lives in R/model_imm.R.

title: 4  Example models
text:
4.1.1 Model definition


R/model_imm.R

.model_imm <- function(resp_error = NULL, nt_features = NULL, nt_distances = NULL,
                       set_size = NULL, regex = FALSE, version = "full", links = NULL,
                       call = NULL, ...) {
  out <- structure(
    list(
      resp_vars = nlist(resp_error),
      other_vars = nlist(nt_features, nt_distances, set_size),
      domain = "Visual working memory",
      task = "Continuous reproduction",
      name = "Interference measurement model by Oberauer and Lin (2017).",
      citation = glue(
        "Oberauer, K., & Lin, H.-Y. (2017). An interference model \\
          of visual working memory. Psychological Review, 124(1), 21-59. \\
          https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000044"
      ),
      version = version,
      requirements = glue(
        "- The response vairable should be in radians and \\
          represent the angular error relative to the target
          - The non-target features should be in radians and be \\
          centered relative to the target"
      ),
      parameters = list(
        mu1 = glue(
          "Location parameter of the von Mises distribution for memory \\
            responses (in radians). Fixed internally to 0 by default."
        ),
        kappa = "Concentration parameter of the von Mises distribution",
        a = "General activation of memory items",
        c = "Context activation",
        s = "Spatial similarity gradient"
      ),
      links = list(
        mu1 = "tan_half",
        kappa = "log",
        a = "log",
        c = "log",
        s = "log"
      ),
      fixed_parameters = list(mu1 = 0, mu2 = 0, kappa2 = -100),
      default_priors = list(
        mu1 = list(main = "normal(0, 0.5)", effects = "normal(0, 0.25)", sd = "exponential(4)"),
        kappa = list(main = "normal(2, 1)", effects = "normal(0, 1)", sd = "exponential(1)"),
        a = list(main = "normal(0, 1)", effects = "normal(0, 1)", sd = "exponential(1)"),
        c = list(main = "normal(0, 1)", effects = "normal(0, 1)", sd = "exponential(1)"),
        s = list(main = "normal(0, 1)", effects = "normal(0, 1)", sd = "exponential(1)")
      ),
      # central 50% of the main default prior on the native scale
      init_ranges = list(
        mu1 = c(-0.65, 0.65),
        kappa = c(3.8, 15),
        a = c(0.51, 2),
        c = c(0.51, 2),
        s = c(0.51, 2)
      )
    ),
    # attributes
    regex = regex,
    regex_vars = c("nt_features", "nt_distances"),
    class = c("bmmodel", "circular", "non_targets", "imm", paste0("imm_", version)),
    call = call
  )

  # add version specific information
  if (version == "abc") {
    out$parameters$s <- NULL
    out$links$s <- NULL
    out$default_priors$s <- NULL
    out$init_ranges$s <- NULL
    attributes(out)$regex_vars <- c("nt_features")
  } else if (version == "bsc") {
    out$parameters$a <- NULL
    out$links$a <- NULL
    out$default_priors$a <- NULL
    out$init_ranges$a <- NULL
  }

  out <- set_links(out, links)
  out
}

The fields are described in Chapter 3. What the IMM adds:

Versions without a version table. The IMM predates version tables. It builds the full specification and then removes parameters for the bsc and abc versions. New models use a version table instead (Section A.6).
More response information than one column. other_vars names the non-target feature and distance columns and the set size; with regex = TRUE the user can give a pattern instead of the column names.
Fixed parameters that identify the model. mu2 and kappa2 are fixed internally. mu1 is in both fixed_parameters and parameters, so it is fixed by default and users may estimate it by giving it a formula.
Links that cannot be changed. The IMM writes its links into the mixture family and the non-linear formulas, so settable_links.imm() returns character(0) and a link a user passes is refused (Section A.1).



4.1.2 check_data() and the dispatch chain
The bsc and full versions need an extra check of the distance columns:


R/model_imm.R

#' @export
check_data.imm_bsc <- function(model, data, formula) {
  data <- .check_data_imm_dist(model, data, formula)
  NextMethod("check_data")
}

#' @export
check_data.imm_full <- function(model, data, formula) {
  data <- .check_data_imm_dist(model, data, formula)
  NextMethod("check_data")
}

.check_data_imm_dist <- function(model, data, formula) {
  nt_distances <- model$other_vars$nt_distances
  max_set_size <- attr(data, "max_set_size")

  stopif(
    !isTRUE(all.equal(length(nt_distances), max_set_size - 1)),
    "The number of columns for non-target distances in the argument \\
    'nt_distances' should equal max(set_size)-1})"
  )

  # replace NA values with 999 so they have 0 effect through the distance formula
  data[, nt_distances][is.na(data[, nt_distances])] <- 999

  stopif(
    any(data[, nt_distances] < 0),
    "All non-target distances to the target need to be postive."
  )
  data
}

Everything else is inherited. For imm_full, with class c("bmmodel", "circular", "non_targets", "imm", "imm_full"), the methods run in this order:

check_data.bmmodel(): the data can be coerced to a data frame and has rows; sets the data_name and checked attributes.
check_data.circular(): the response is in radians, wrapped to \((-\pi, \pi]\).
check_data.non_targets(): checks nt_features and set_size, creates index variables, and stores max_set_size and lure_idx_vars as data attributes.
No method exists for imm, so dispatch passes on.
check_data.imm_full(): checks nt_distances.

General methods run first, so the model’s own method can rely on their work: by the time check_data.imm_full() runs, max_set_size is already an attribute. A new circular model with non-targets inherits all of these checks and only writes its own.


4.1.3 configure_model()


R/model_imm.R

configure_model.imm_full <- function(model, data, formula) {
  # retrieve arguments from the data check
  max_set_size <- attr(data, "max_set_size")
  lure_idx <- attr(data, "lure_idx_vars")
  nt_features <- model$other_vars$nt_features
  nt_distances <- model$other_vars$nt_distances

  formula <- .base_imm_formula(model, formula) +
    brms::nlf(theta1 ~ log(exp(c) + exp(a))) +
    brms::nlf(expS ~ exp(s))

  theta_exprs <- glue("{lure_idx} * log(exp(c-expS*{nt_distances}) + exp(a)) + (1 - {lure_idx}) * (-100)")
  formula <- .add_imm_mixture_terms(formula, max_set_size, lure_idx, nt_features, theta_exprs)
  formula$family <- .imm_mixture_family(max_set_size)

  nlist(formula, data)
}

The method reads what check_data() stored (Section 3.6), builds the formula with bmf2bf(), adds the non-linear terms and sets the family. It returns no stanvars, because brms::mixture() needs no Stan code from bmm.
The three IMM versions differ only in the theta expression, so what they share lives in private helpers:


R/model_imm.R

.base_imm_formula <- function(model, formula) {
  bmf2bf(model, formula) +
    brms::lf(kappa2 ~ 1) +
    brms::lf(mu2 ~ 1) +
    brms::nlf(kappa1 ~ kappa)
}

.add_imm_mixture_terms <- function(formula, max_set_size, lure_idx, nt_features, theta_exprs) {
  kappa_nts <- paste0("kappa", 3:(max_set_size + 1))
  theta_nts <- paste0("theta", 3:(max_set_size + 1))
  mu_nts <- paste0("mu", 3:(max_set_size + 1))

  for (i in 1:(max_set_size - 1)) {
    formula <- formula +
      glue_nlf("{kappa_nts[i]} ~ kappa") +
      glue_nlf("{theta_nts[i]} ~ {theta_exprs[i]}") +
      glue_nlf("{mu_nts[i]} ~ {nt_features[i]}")
  }

  formula
}

.imm_mixture_family <- function(max_set_size) {
  brms::mixture(
    brms::von_mises("tan_half"), brms::von_mises("identity"),
    nmix = c(1, max_set_size),
    order = "none"
  )
}

Each version builds theta_exprs, one expression per non-target position, and passes it to .add_imm_mixture_terms(). This is the pattern to copy when your versions share a formula skeleton: put the skeleton in a helper prefixed with a dot, and let each version supply what differs. Do not start a helper’s name with .model_, because model_names() lists every object with that prefix as a model.


4.1.4 From bmmformula to brmsformula
bmf2bf() builds the first line of the brms formula from the response and adds one component per parameter. Most models use the default:


R/bmmformula.R

# If no model specific methods exist, it will construct a base brms formula from the first resp_vars
# We do it this way because most models require just one response variable
#' @export
bmf2bf.bmmodel <- function(model, formula = bmmformula()) {
  brms_formula <- NextMethod("bmf2bf") %||% brms::bf(glue("{model$resp_vars[[1]]} ~ 1"))
  components <- lapply(formula, function(x) if (is_nl(x)) brms::nlf(x) else brms::lf(x))
  Reduce(`+`, components, init = brms_formula)
}

#' @export
bmf2bf.default <- function(model, formula) {
  NULL
}

bmf2bf.bmmodel() runs first, because "bmmodel" is first in the class vector, and asks the rest of the chain for a first line through NextMethod(). If no model method answers, bmf2bf.default() returns NULL and bmf2bf.bmmodel() builds resp ~ 1 itself. A model that needs a different first line defines its own method, as the DDM below does. Each parameter formula then becomes brms::nlf() if one of its predictors is also a parameter and brms::lf() otherwise.

title: 4  Example models
text:
4.2 The Diffusion Decision Model (DDM)
The DDM lives in R/model_ddm.R.

4.2.1 Model definition


R/model_ddm.R

.ddm_defaults <- list(
  parameters = list(
    drift = "Drift rate = Average rate of evidence accumulation of the decision processes",
    bound = "Boundary separation = Distance between the decision boundaries that need to be reached",
    ndt   = "Non-decision time = Additional time required beyond the evidence accumulation process",
    zr    = "Relative starting point = Starting point as a proportion of the boundary separation, measured from the lower boundary (0.5 = unbiased, > 0.5 = biased towards the upper response)."
  ),
  links = list(
    drift = "identity", bound = "log", ndt = "log", zr = "logit"
  ),
  fixed_parameters = list(
    zr = 0,
    mu = 0
  ),
  priors = list(
    drift = list(main = "cauchy(0,1)", effects = "normal(0,0.5)", sd = "exponential(1)"),
    bound = list(main = "normal(0,0.5)", effects = "normal(0,0.5)", sd = "exponential(2)"),
    ndt   = list(main = "normal(-1.5,0.5)", effects = "normal(0,0.3)", sd = "exponential(2)"),
    zr    = list(main = "normal(0,0.5)", effects = "normal(0,0.3)", sd = "exponential(2)")
  ),
  init_ranges = list(
    mu = c(-0.1,0.1),
    drift  = c(-1,1),
    bound  = c(1,2),
    ndt    = c(0.01,0.05),
    zr     = c(0.45,0.55)
  )
)

.model_ddm <- function(rt = NULL, response = NULL, links = NULL, call = NULL, ...) {
  out <- structure(
    list(
      resp_vars = nlist(rt, response),
      other_vars = nlist(),
      domain = "Decision Making / Response times",
      task = "Two-Alternative Force Choice RT",
      name = "Diffusion Decision Model",
      citation = glue(
        "Ratcliff, R. (1978). A theory of memory retrieval. Psychological \\
        Review, 85(2), 59-108. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.85.2.59"
      ),
      version = "NA",
      requirements = glue(
        "- The response time should be in seconds and \\
          represent the time between onset of the target stimulus until the response execution
          - The response should be coded numerically: \\
          0 = lower response, 1 = upper response"
      ),
      parameters = .ddm_defaults[["parameters"]],
      links = .ddm_defaults[["links"]],
      fixed_parameters = .ddm_defaults[["fixed_parameters"]],
      default_priors = .ddm_defaults[["priors"]],
      init_ranges = .ddm_defaults[["init_ranges"]]
    ),
    class = c("bmmodel", "ddm"),
    call = call
  )
  out <- set_links(out, links)
  out
}

This is the layout use_model_template() generates: the specification in .ddm_defaults, read field by field by the constructor. The DDM differs from the IMM in three ways:

No natural mu. The family gets a dummy mu, fixed to 0 through fixed_parameters and left out of parameters (Section A.2).
Two response variables, rt and response, which need their own first formula line.
init_ranges keep the non-decision time below the fastest response at the start of sampling (Section A.3).

Its class chain is short, c("bmmodel", "ddm"), because the response time models share few data checks.


4.2.2 bmf2bf()


R/model_ddm.R

#' @export
bmf2bf.ddm <- function(model, formula) {
  rt <- model$resp_vars$rt
  response <- model$resp_vars$response
  brms::bf(paste0(rt, " | dec(", response, ") ~ 1"))
}

This produces rt | dec(response) ~ 1, where dec() tells brms which column codes the decision (0 = lower, 1 = upper boundary).


4.2.3 configure_model()


R/model_ddm.R

#' @export
configure_model.ddm <- function(model, data, formula) {
  formula <- bmf2bf(model, formula)

  ddm_family <- function(link_drift, link_bound, link_ndt, link_zr) {
    brms::custom_family(
      "ddm",
      dpars = c("mu", "drift", "bound", "ndt", "zr"),
      links = c("identity", link_drift, link_bound, link_ndt, link_zr),
      lb = c(NA, NA, 0.1, 0, 0),
      ub = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 1),
      type = "real",
      vars = "dec[n]",
      loop = TRUE,
      log_lik = log_lik_ddm,
      posterior_predict = posterior_predict_ddm,
      posterior_epred = posterior_epred_ddm
    )
  }

  formula$family <- ddm_family(
    link_drift = model$links$drift,
    link_bound = model$links$bound,
    link_ndt = model$links$ndt,
    link_zr = model$links$zr
  )

  sc_path <- system.file("stan_chunks", package = "bmm")
  stan_functions <- read_lines2(paste0(sc_path, "/ddm_functions.stan"))
  stanvars <- brms::stanvar(scode = stan_functions, block = "functions")

  nlist(formula, data, stanvars)
}

The pieces of a custom family:

dpars lists the dummy mu first, with an identity link, then the model parameters with the links from model$links, so a link the user sets reaches the family.
vars = "dec[n]" passes the decision column to the Stan likelihood. brms connects the family to Stan by name: the family "ddm" calls ddm_lpdf(), defined in inst/stan_chunks/ddm_functions.stan, which configure_model() reads and passes as stanvars.
log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred are plain R functions (Chapter 6). The first two are built on dddm() and rddm() from R/distributions.R; posterior_epred_ddm() returns the expected response time.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
What use_model_template() does
If you have read Section 3 and Section 4, you should have a pretty good idea of how the bmm package functions. Now it’s time to add your new model.
You don’t have to create the files by hand. use_model_template() generates the model file with stubs for every method a model needs, so you can focus on filling them in. The chapter ends with a checklist of everything a new model has to touch outside its own file, because the test suite fails on some of those and review catches the rest.
Run it from the root of the package. It writes R/model_<model_name>.R containing the parameter specification, the model constructor, the user-facing alias, and stub methods for check_data, bmf2bf, configure_model and postprocess_brm. With custom_family = TRUE it also creates one empty inst/stan_chunks/<model_name>_<block>.stan file per entry in stanvar_blocks, wires the code that reads them into configure_model, and adds empty log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred functions that the family already points to.
The full argument list is on the reference page for use_model_template(). Three things about the call are worth knowing:

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
versions is the second positional argument. use_model_template("gcm", TRUE) means versions = TRUE, not custom_family = TRUE. Name the arguments.
The stan files are created before the R file is written. If the call fails partway through, empty .stan files are already on disk and you have to remove them by hand before you can call the function again.
An unversioned model gets version = "NA" — the literal string, not NA.


What the template leaves for you
The generated file follows the package’s conventions. Two things in it are placeholders that check() will not flag:

The prediction functions are empty. With custom_family = TRUE, the family passes log_lik_<model>(), posterior_predict_<model>() and posterior_epred_<model>() to brms, but their bodies are empty, so loo(), pp_check() and posterior_epred() cannot work on your model until you fill them (step 8 below).
The settable_links stub is commented out. Uncomment it, so that its tag line reads #' @exportS3Method, if configure_model() builds links into the family or the formulas; otherwise delete it (step 2 below).

There are no stubs for check_formula(), configure_prior(), create_initfun(), revert_check_data() or the optional post-fit methods; add those only if your model needs them.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.1 Example
Let’s add a new model called gcm. Assume you have tested the model in Stan and have the Stan code ready. We want a custom family with two Stan blocks, likelihood and functions (see ?brms::stanvar for the blocks).
First set up your system and git environment as described in Section 1. Then load the development version with devtools::load_all() and run, from the root directory of the bmm package:
use_model_template("gcm", custom_family = TRUE, stanvar_blocks = c("likelihood", "functions"))
This creates R/model_gcm.R and the empty files inst/stan_chunks/gcm_likelihood.stan and inst/stan_chunks/gcm_functions.stan, and opens them in your editor. The top of the R file holds the specification and the constructor:
.gcm_defaults <- list(
  parameters = list(
    par1 = "Parameter 1 = description of parameter 1",
    par2 = "Parameter 2 = description of parameter 2"
  ),
  links = list(
    par1 = "identity",
    par2 = "log"
  ),
  fixed_parameters = list(
    mu = 0
  ),
  # pick the sd rate by meaning: 1 for sensitivity, strength, concentration
  # (kappa), mixing weights and identity-linked drift; 2 for criteria,
  # thresholds, boundary, ndt, start point, log-linked drift, diffusion
  # constant, log ratios, log SDs and correlations; 4 for circular bias
  priors = list(
    par1 = list(main = "normal(0, 1)", effects = "normal(0, 0.5)", sd = "exponential(1)"),
    par2 = list(main = "normal(0, 0.5)", effects = "normal(0, 0.5)", sd = "exponential(2)")
  ),
  init_ranges = list(
    par1 = c(-1, 1),
    par2 = c(0.5, 1.5)
  )
)


.model_gcm <- function(resp_var1 = NULL, required_arg1 = NULL, required_arg2 = NULL,
                                  links = NULL, call = NULL, ...) {
  out <- structure(
    list(
      resp_vars = nlist(resp_var1),
      other_vars = nlist(required_arg1, required_arg2),
      domain = "",
      task = "",
      name = "",
      citation = character(),
      version = "NA",
      requirements = "",
      parameters = .gcm_defaults[["parameters"]],
      links = .gcm_defaults[["links"]],
      fixed_parameters = .gcm_defaults[["fixed_parameters"]],
      default_priors = .gcm_defaults[["priors"]],
      init_ranges = .gcm_defaults[["init_ranges"]]
    ),
    class = c("bmmodel", "gcm"),
    call = call
  )
  out <- set_links(out, links)
  out
}

# uncomment if configure_model() builds the links into the family or into
# the non-linear formulas rather than reading them from the list above,
# so that a link set by the user is refused instead of silently ignored:
# #' @exportS3Method
# settable_links.gcm <- function(model) character(0)
Above the specification, a header comment lists the registries outside the file that a new model must update and the format citation must follow. One line of that header is out of date in bmm 1.4.1: the stored-frame test case no longer goes into stored_frame_cases() in test-update.R but into your model’s test-case file (see Testing). The other entries, data_column_roles, revert_check_data(), response_annotations() and the citation format, are correct. Below it come the user-facing alias gcm() with its roxygen block, and the stubs check_data.gcm(), bmf2bf.gcm(), configure_model.gcm() (with a custom_family() skeleton and the lines that read your two Stan files), log_lik_gcm(), posterior_predict_gcm(), posterior_epred_gcm() and postprocess_brm.gcm(). The check_data, bmf2bf and postprocess_brm stubs carry a header comment saying when you may delete them.
For a complete model written to the current conventions, read R/model_sdt_yn.R: a custom family on aggregated counts, with its own log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred functions and a settable_links method. Most of its length is documentation.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.2 Filling in the template

The specification and the constructor. Most of your work is in .gcm_defaults: the parameters (with descriptions), their links, which parameters are fixed and to what value, the default priors, and the initialization ranges. Set default priors (main, effects and sd) for every parameter, informed by knowledge in the field; .ddm_defaults in R/model_ddm.R is a worked example. Give init_ranges only to parameters whose likelihood is undefined in part of their range, such as a non-decision time that must stay below the fastest RT (see Section A.3). Prefer parameter names of more than one letter that do not match a likely data column (see Failure modes to expect).
In .model_gcm(), rename the response and required arguments and fill in the metadata (domain, task, name, citation, requirements). citation holds one reference per element, each on a single line, without a - bullet, and ending in . or a https://doi.org/ URL; model_citation() hands them to users for their reference lists. Two more things about the constructor are checked by tests: it must run with no arguments (the tests call every .model_*() bare, which is why every argument defaults to NULL), and its fields must stay in the order the template emits them. For domain, reuse the string of the models your model sits with, so that bmm_models() and the website list it under the right task group: "Visual working memory", "Working Memory (categorical), Categorical Decision Making", "Categorical decision making, memory, and reasoning" (MPT), "Perception & Recognition Memory" (or "Recognition Memory", which lands in the same group) or "Decision Making / Response times". A new string becomes a group of its own.
For a model with several versions, generate the scaffold with use_model_template("gcm", versions = c("v1", "v2")). You get a .gcm_version_table with one entry per version, a constructor that reads each field from it and appends paste0("gcm_", version) to the class, and an alias with version = c("v1", "v2") validated by match.arg(). Keep the default as a literal c(...): model_versions() reads it to build the per-version documentation tables.
Links. The constructor passes the user’s links through set_links(), which refuses names that are not parameters, repairs one-letter typos with a warning, and warns when a link widens the parameter’s range (say identity instead of log). By default every link in your links list can be changed by the user. If configure_model() writes a link into the family, the Stan code or the non-linear formulas instead of reading it from the list, a user’s choice would be silently ignored, so declare which links can be set:
#' @exportS3Method
settable_links.gcm <- function(model) character(0)   # or c("par1")
Name the method for your model class, not for bmmodel, which comes first in every class vector and would shadow it. A model that substitutes the inverse link into its formulas itself also overrides settable_link_functions(); the multinomial SDT models are the examples.
The user-facing alias. Rename the required arguments and fill in @examples with a full example. Keep the generated @keywords bmmodel: the pkgdown test needs it and is skipped inside check() (see Chapter 6). Title and details are generated from the constructor.
check_data.gcm() checks the data and returns it, ending with NextMethod("check_data"). It may compute transformations or store values as data attributes for configure_model (see Section 3.6). If it adds, renames or packs columns, update() needs to undo that before it can re-run it on a fitted model’s data; see Section 3.7.
bmf2bf.gcm(), if needed. You need a custom method if your model has several response variables (DDM: rt | dec(response) ~ 1), uses aggregate data through vreal(), vint() or trials() (EZDM, sdt_yn), or needs other response wrapping. brms reads this formula as the linear model for the family’s mu. If your model has no natural mu, suppress it: put mu = 0 in fixed_parameters, add a dummy mu (identity link) to the family’s dpars, and write the first formula line yourself (see Section A.2). Leave the dummy mu out of parameters, so that prior_info() and parameter_info() do not report it.
configure_model.gcm() builds the formula, the family and the stanvars and returns nlist(formula, data, stanvars). It does not return initial values. brms connects the family to your Stan code by name: a custom family "gcm" with dpars = c("mu", "par1", "par2") calls a Stan function gcm_lpdf(y | mu, par1, par2) (gcm_lpmf for an integer response) that you define in gcm_functions.stan. The DDM method in Chapter 4 shows the whole pattern, and the brms custom families vignette explains it. Add further Stan files to inst/stan_chunks/ and read them here. If your Stan code has to differ when the user asks for within-chain threading, see Section A.5.
postprocess_brm.gcm() changes the fitted object (renaming parameters and the like). Delete the section if you need none. If you keep it, also write revert_postprocess_brm.gcm(), which undoes the change: update() calls it to get the fit back into the shape brms built before refitting. R/model_sdm.R has both.
log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred, for a custom family. These are plain R functions passed to brms::custom_family(); the template generates them empty and already passes them to the family, and their contracts are in Chapter 6. They power LOO and WAIC, posterior predictive checks, and posterior_epred()/fitted(). Build them on d*() and r*() functions for your model in R/distributions.R, which you write first (see Distribution functions). If the mean of your response is not a useful quantity, pass posterior_epred_undefined("gcm"), as SDM does, so the user gets an error that points to native_parameters(). Models built on a native brms family (brms::mixture(), brms::multinomial()) get all three from brms.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.3 Testing
A new model adds two files to tests/testthat/:

test-model_gcm.R tests your model’s own contract: constructor validation, check_data(), configure_model(), the content of the generated Stan code, and your d*/r* functions. tests/testthat/test-model_ddm.R and test-model_sdt_yn.R are examples.
helper-model-gcm.R registers your model with the tests that run over every model (default priors, initial values, update(), links, posterior predictive checks). It defines one function, model_cases_gcm(), which returns small cases those tests use. A stored_frame, an sd_default, an init and a links case are required; check_data, observables and fixture cases apply only to some models. Copy tests/testthat/helper-model-ddm.R and adapt it. For a model without random-effect quirks or extra observables, it looks like this:
model_cases_gcm <- function() {
  model <- gcm("resp", "exemplar", "category")
  data <- toy_gcm_data()  # write a small dataset next to those in helper-model-data.R
  re_formula <- bmf(par1 ~ 1 + (1 | id), par2 ~ 1 + (1 | id))
  list(
    stored_frame = list(gcm = list(model = model, formula = bmf(par1 ~ 1, par2 ~ 1), data = data)),
    sd_default = list(gcm = list(
      model = model, formula = re_formula, data = data,
      sd = c(par1 = "exponential(1)", par2 = "exponential(2)")
    )),
    init = list(gcm = list(model = model, formula = re_formula, data = data)),
    links = list(gcm = list(model = model, settable = c("par1", "par2")))
  )
}
sd repeats your default sd priors and settable what settable_links() returns. The header of helper-model-cases.R describes the optional cases.

Tests must not sample, so pipeline tests use brms’ mock backend. backend = "mock" is a brms::brm() argument, and whatever you pass as mock_fit is returned in place of the fitted Stan object. Everything before the fit (data checks, formula, family, Stan code, priors, initial values) runs for real, which is what you want to test:
test_that("gcm model runs without errors", {
  withr::local_options("bmm.silent" = 2)
  skip_on_cran()

  dat <- data.frame(
    resp = rnorm(10),
    exemplar = rep(c("A", "B"), 5),
    category = rep(c(1, 2), each = 5)
  )

  f <- bmmformula(par1 ~ 1, par2 ~ 1)
  mock_fit <- bmm(
    f, dat,
    gcm(resp_var1 = "resp", required_arg1 = "exemplar", required_arg2 = "category"),
    backend = "mock", mock_fit = 1, rename = FALSE
  )
  expect_equal(mock_fit$fit, 1)
})
Every argument of the alias without a default has to be supplied, because the alias calls stop_missing_args(). Older test files write mock = 1, which works only because R partial-matches it to mock_fit.
The rest of the rules are numbered R1 to R10 in bmm’s AGENTS.md, with the reasoning in ADR 0004. The ones a new model meets:

Seed with withr::local_seed(), never set.seed().
A test that compiles Stan code opens with skip_unless_stan_tests(). A test that takes more than 0.4 s with NOT_CRAN unset on your machine opens with skip_on_cran(), so that the package’s check stays within CRAN’s time limit.
The suite has a time budget. Check your tests with devtools::test(reporter = "slow").
tests/testthat/test-conventions.R checks several of these rules and fails with the rule’s number.

tests/testthat/helper-epred.R has epred_vs_predict() and expect_epred_by_cell() for testing a posterior_epred function against posterior_predict. If your Stan code changes with threading, test the generated code with and without it (Section A.5).

5.3.1 Parameter recovery
A new model needs a parameter recovery study on simulated data. The pull request description shows true against recovered values, as a table or a plot, from a hierarchical design with several subjects whose parameters vary, on data simulated with an independent generator rather than your own r* function. Attach the script as a gist or in a collapsed block. Chapter 6 explains why the generator matters, and CONTRIBUTING.md has the requirements.


5.3.2 Distribution functions
A custom family also needs distribution functions in R/distributions.R: d* and r*, optionally p* and q*. They simulate data, back log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred, and drive the plots. Write them before the prediction functions.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.5 Failure modes to expect

configure_prior() errors when fixed_parameters names a parameter the formula never gets. Every fixed parameter has to be wired into the formula by configure_model(). The usual cause is mu = 0 without a dummy mu in the family (Section A.2).
Method signatures must match the generics. create_initfun() receives the prior as its fourth argument, and configure_prior() methods receive data2, knots or drop_unused_levels through ... when the user passes them; a method without ... fails only in that case. R CMD check reports both.
Short parameter names collide with Stan parameter names and data columns. Prefer names of more than one letter (Section A.8).

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.6 Post-processing
Most post-fit tools read the model object and need no code from you. native_parameters(), parameter_info() and prior_info() read the specification; conditional_effects() and emmeans() work through the bmmfit class; posterior_epred() and fitted() call your family’s posterior_epred function; pp_check() checks the response, and further observables if you declared them; bmm_data_check() runs your check_data() without compiling.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.7 Add an example dataset
Every new model needs an example dataset that users can load and that the examples use: a new dataset added to the package, one already in it, or one from another package loaded with data(). The IMM and the SDT models use datasets shipped with bmm; the mixture2p and mixture3p articles use data('bays2009_full', package = 'mixtur'). R Packages explains how to add one.

title: 5  Adding a new model
text:
5.8 Add an article
Every new model needs an article explaining the model and how to fit it. Create it with usethis::use_article(); the existing ones are in vignettes/articles/, and the published versions are here. Articles load their fits from cached files, which are not committed; CONTRIBUTING.md says how to hand over the fit. The README, the home page and the Get started tables list your model automatically, from its constructor and its data_column_roles entry.

title: 6  Coding conventions
text:
6.1 Errors, warnings and messages
This chapter is the reference for how bmm code is written. Your pull request will be judged against these conventions. The Coding style section of bmm’s CONTRIBUTING.md and its AGENTS.md state them briefly; this chapter gives the reasons.
Read it as conventions, not as a style war. Most of the entries have a reason attached, and the reason is usually that the alternative broke something.
Use the package’s own helpers rather than the base functions:
The base functions survive almost only inside the definitions of the helpers themselves and in R/brms-misc.R, which is vendored code: a copy of brms internals kept inside bmm rather than called through brms::, and marked read-only. sprintf() is still the right tool for formatting numbers ("%.2f"); the rule is about building messages.
Two of the reasons deserve spelling out, because they are not stylistic.
message2() checks getOption("bmm.silent", 1) and prints nothing at silence level 2 or above. Tests set withr::local_options("bmm.silent" = 2) to keep output clean. A base message() call ignores that and will make somebody’s test noisy.
stopif() and warnif() pass env.frame = -2 down to stop2(). That number counts frames back up the call stack: -1 would interpolate in stopif()’s own frame, where your variables do not exist, so -2 reaches past it into the function that called stopif(). This is what lets the message interpolate variables from your function. So this works and needs no glue() call of its own:
Write messages as one glue string. stop2() handles multi-line strings with trailing \\ continuations, so a long message does not need paste0().
