title: 6  Coding conventions
text:
6.2 Dependencies
Package code is base R plus the native pipe |>. bmm requires R >= 4.1.0, so |> is always available and %>% is not used in package code.
The Imports in DESCRIPTION are a short list, and adding to it needs a reason the reviewer will accept. dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2 and stringr are Suggests, not Imports — dplyr and tidyr became optional in 1.2.0, and magrittr was removed in 1.3.0. If you have seen bmm guidance that prescribes dplyr idiom for package code, it is out of date. Tidyverse packages belong in articles and tests, where they are already available.
A function from a Suggests package must be guarded, or the package breaks for anyone who installed it without that suggestion. The pattern is:
stopif(
  !requireNamespace("tidyr", quietly = TRUE),
  'The "tidyr" package is required for this functionality'
)
data <- tidyr::gather(data, non_target_name, non_target_value, eval(nt_features))
as in R/helpers-data.R. Note the same function opens with
y <- y_nt <- non_target_name <- non_target_value <- NULL
which exists to silence R CMD check’s “no visible binding for global variable” notes from the non-standard evaluation in the gather() call. If you write code with bare column names, you need this line.
Always namespace explicitly: brms::stanvar(), stats::complete.cases(), methods::formalArgs(). bmm imports few functions directly, and an unqualified call to an Imports package is the kind of thing that works on your machine and fails in R CMD check.

title: 6  Coding conventions
6  Coding conventions
text:
6.4 S3 conventions
Dispatch runs general to specific. A model’s class vector starts with "bmmodel" (the class chains are listed in Section 3.4), so check_data.bmmodel runs before check_data.sdm, not after. This is the opposite of the intuition most people bring, and it has one sharp corollary: a fall-through fallback belongs on .default, never on .bmmodel. A method defined on .bmmodel runs first and shadows nothing, but a fallback placed there would be reached before the model-specific method had a chance to run. bmf2bf is the worked example — bmf2bf.default returns NULL and bmf2bf.bmmodel supplies the fallback after NextMethod() has come back empty (see Chapter 4).
Every check_data method ends with NextMethod("check_data"). Each method does its own model-specific validation and then hands on down the chain. The only method without it is check_data.default, which is the end of the chain and returns the data. Forget it in a method on a shared class (circular, non_targets, sdt) and every more specific method below it never runs, so a model’s own checks are silently skipped. In a model’s own method the omission does no harm today, but the next shared class added above it would break.
Match the generic’s signature exactly, including ... where the generic has one and the defaults on check_model(model, data = NULL, formula = NULL). See the generics table in Chapter 3.

title: 6  Coding conventions
text:
6.5 Where to validate arguments
Validate in the exported constructor only — the user-facing alias. .model_*(), configure_model.*() and private helpers should not, because their error messages name arguments the user never typed. The alias is the one place where the argument the message refers to is the argument the user actually passed:


R/model_m3.R

m3 <- function(resp_cats, num_options, choice_rule = "softmax", version = "custom", ...) {
  call <- match.call()
  stop_missing_args() # errors naming any argument with no default that the user omitted
  stopif(
    length(num_options) != length(resp_cats),
    "The option variables should have the same length as the response variables."
  )
  .model_m3(...)
}

check_data.*() is the exception, and not really an exception: it validates properties of the data, which the constructor cannot see. “Your nt_distances columns contain negative values” is a data message and belongs there.

title: 6  Coding conventions
text:
6.6 log_lik, posterior_predict and posterior_epred
These are plain functions, not S3 methods. Do not name them log_lik.mymodel — that would register them against brms’ log_lik generic, which is not what you want. Name them log_lik_<family_name> and pass them to brms::custom_family():
sdm_simple <- brms::custom_family(
  name = "sdm_simple",
  dpars = c("mu", "c", "kappa"),   # distributional parameters
  ...
  log_lik = log_lik_sdm_simple,
  posterior_predict = posterior_predict_sdm_simple,
  posterior_epred = posterior_epred_sdm_simple
)
brms checks the first arguments when you build the family: log_lik must start with (i, prep) and posterior_predict with (i, prep, ...).
Both take i, the index of one observation, and prep, an object brms assembles from the fitted model and hands to you. prep holds the posterior draws and the data, and you pull values out of it rather than computing them: brms::get_dpar() for a parameter, prep$data$Y for the response.
The contract is easy to get wrong in one specific way. brms::get_dpar(prep, "par", i = i) returns a vector with one value per posterior draw, not a scalar, and your function must return a vector of that same length. The response is a scalar, prep$data$Y[i]:


R/model_sdm.R

log_lik_sdm_simple <- function(i, prep) {
  mu <- brms::get_dpar(prep, "mu", i = i)
  c <- brms::get_dpar(prep, "c", i = i)
  kappa <- brms::get_dpar(prep, "kappa", i = i)
  y <- prep$data$Y[i]
  dsdm(y, mu, c, kappa, log = T)
}

A density function that collapses its arguments (an if on a vector, a sum()) will return a scalar here, and brms will recycle it across all draws without complaint. The posterior predictive checks then look suspiciously clean. Check length() of what you return.
posterior_epred_<family_name> has a different contract: it takes only prep, is called once for all observations, and returns a draws × observations matrix of expected responses. prep$dpars then holds one draws × observations matrix per parameter, and data columns have to be lined up with them. Two helpers in R/helpers-postprocess.R do the bookkeeping: .epred_data() repeats a data column per draw, and .epred_matrix() shapes the result:


R/model_sdt_yn.R

posterior_epred_sdt_yn <- function(prep) {
  stimulus <- .epred_data(prep$data$vint1, prep)
  dist <- .sdt_dist_names[prep$data$vint2[1]]
  criterion <- .sdt_criterion_dpar(prep, prep$dpars$d, prep$dpars$sdratio)
  p_old <- with(prep$dpars, exp(.sdt_log_p_old(.sdt_eta(d, criterion, stimulus, sdratio), dist)))
  .epred_matrix(.epred_data(prep$data$trials, prep) * p_old, prep)
}

Pass it to custom_family() like the other two. A custom family without one fails in posterior_epred() with “object ‘posterior_epred_’ not found”, because brms looks for the function in the global environment. If the expected response of your model is not meaningful, pass posterior_epred_undefined("<model>"), which fails with a message pointing to native_parameters().
For a custom family on aggregated data, loop and vars decide what the Stan likelihood can index; see Section A.4. The names you give a family’s parameters have traps of their own (Section A.8).

title: 6  Coding conventions
section: 6.7 Documentation and the checks that enforce it
text:
6.7 Documentation and the checks that enforce it
NAMESPACE and everything in man/ are generated. Run devtools::document(); never hand-edit them.
Exported functions need @returns and @examples. Two further requirements are enforced by tests rather than by review:
@keywords. The package website is built by pkgdown, which needs every public help topic to appear somewhere in its reference index, and _pkgdown.yml is where that index is declared. tests/testthat/test-pkgdown.R reads every man/*.Rd file, drops the ones with \keyword{internal}, and fails if any remaining topic is not covered by the reference section of _pkgdown.yml. Coverage can be by name or through a has_keyword() selector, and _pkgdown.yml has has_keyword("bmmodel"). So a new model’s user-facing alias needs #' @keywords bmmodel, which every model alias carries and which use_model_template() generates. Keep it when you edit the roxygen block. An exported function that is not a model gets @keywords internal or a place in _pkgdown.yml.
A NEWS bullet for every user-visible change, under the development heading at the top of NEWS.md (on a dev-x.y.0 branch, under that release’s heading), with the issue or pull request number in parentheses. Keep it short: what changes for the user and what they should do, not how the fix works.

title: 6  Coding conventions
text:
6.8 Tests
Test files mirror source file names: R/model_ddm.R is tested by tests/testthat/test-model_ddm.R. Some files cover a theme instead (test-default-priors.R, test-pkgdown.R). Tests use testthat edition 3, the mock backend instead of sampling, and withr::local_options("bmm.silent" = 2) so that message2() output does not clutter the run. The rules that apply to every test are numbered R1 to R10 in AGENTS.md; Chapter 5 lists the ones a new model meets.

title: 6  Coding conventions
text:
6.9 Parameter recovery: the circularity trap
What a recovery study for a new model has to show is set out in CONTRIBUTING.md: true against recovered values, a hierarchical design with several subjects, and data from an independent generator. The last point is the one that is easy to get wrong.
Do not simulate and fit with the same distribution function. If you generate data with your own rmymodel() and fit a likelihood built from your own dmymodel(), the study reports clean recovery whether or not either function is correct, because any error shared by both cancels. Use an independent generator: rtdists::rdiffusion() for diffusion-type models (rtdists is already in Imports), a published reference implementation, or a direct simulation of the process the model describes. A recovery study that cannot fail is not evidence.

title: Appendix A — Reference
text:
A.1 Links
This appendix collects details you need only in particular situations. Each section starts by saying when that is.
You need this when your model’s links cannot all be changed by the user, or when a user reports that a link they set had no effect.
bmm implements the links "identity", "log", "softplus", "log1p", "logm1", "inverse", "sqrt", "logit", "probit", "cloglog" and "tan_half". A model may also declare "loglog" or "softmax" as its own default, but users cannot ask for them. "softplus" is an alternative to "log" for positive parameters: it grows linearly rather than exponentially, so predictor effects are additive on the natural scale and large values do not overflow.
The constructor assigns the user’s links with set_links(). It refuses a name that is not a parameter (a one-letter typo is repaired, with a warning), refuses a link the model cannot apply, and warns when the new link admits values the default excludes, such as identity for a positive parameter. check_model() runs the same validation on links assigned after construction.
By default every link can be changed. A model that writes its links into the family, the Stan code or the non-linear formulas, instead of reading them from model$links at fit time, must say so with a settable_links() method that returns character(0) or the subset that works. Otherwise a user’s link would show in print() and in the priors while the sampler ignored it. SDM, the mixture models and the IMM return character(0); the SDT models return the parameters whose links reach the likelihood. A model that substitutes the inverse link into its formulas itself also overrides settable_link_functions(), as M3, MPT and the multinomial SDT models do.

title: Appendix A — Reference
section: A.2 Models without a location parameter
text:
A.2 Models without a location parameter
You need this when your model has no natural mu, as is typical for response time models.
brms requires every custom family to have a mu parameter. DDM, EZDM and cswald have none, and suppress it rather than promote one of their parameters to it:

The family’s dpars include a dummy mu with an identity link.
fixed_parameters contains mu = 0.
mu is left out of parameters, so prior_info() and parameter_info() do not report it, and users do not give it a formula.
The model’s bmf2bf() method writes the first formula line itself, such as rt | dec(response) ~ 1 for the DDM.

If you add mu = 0 to fixed_parameters but forget the dummy mu in dpars, configure_prior() errors, because every fixed parameter has to exist in the formula.

title: Appendix A — Reference
text:
A.3 Initial values
You need this when chains fail at initialization or diverge immediately, typically because the likelihood is undefined for part of a parameter’s range.
brms’ default initialization draws every parameter from a wide symmetric range on the sampling scale. For a non-decision time that must stay below the fastest observed RT, that often starts chains where the likelihood is undefined. init_ranges gives such parameters a narrow window on the native scale:
init_ranges = list(
  mu    = c(-0.1, 0.1),
  drift = c(-1, 1),
  bound = c(1, 2),
  ndt   = c(0.01, 0.05)
)
create_initfun.default() in R/helpers-inits.R reads the parameter dimensions from the Stan code and builds an initialization function:

Random effects start tight: standard deviations between 0.05 and 0.1, standardized effects near zero, correlation matrices at the identity.
Population-level parameters with an init_ranges entry start inside that range. The range is transformed through the parameter’s link (for softmax mixing weights it is already on the sampling scale), so it stays valid when the user changes the link. With predictors, the coefficients are solved so that each design cell starts inside the range.
Everything else gets brms’ default draw.

create_initfun() maps Stan parameter names back to model parameters with the regular expression (^|_)param(_|$), taking the longest match. A parameter called s therefore matches b_s_Intercept but not b_sim_Intercept. A name that appears as a whole underscore-delimited token elsewhere in the Stan parameter names is not safe.

title: Appendix A — Reference
text:
A.4 Aggregated data and vars
You need this when your model is fitted to counts or summary statistics instead of one row per trial.
brms has special response terms that pass further columns to the Stan likelihood: vreal() for real values, vint() for integers and trials() for a trial count. The EZDM’s bmf2bf() method builds mean_rt | vreal(var_rt) + vint(n_upper) + trials(n_trials) ~ 1, which makes the columns available in Stan as vreal1[n], vint1[n] and trials[n]. The family names them in vars:
brms::custom_family(..., loop = TRUE, vars = c("vreal1[n]", "vint1[n]", "trials[n]"))
loop decides the shape of the generated Stan code. With loop = TRUE, brms emits one likelihood call per observation; with loop = FALSE, one vectorized call. You may index vars with [n] only in a looped likelihood; otherwise brms stops with “Invalid use of index ‘[n]’ in an unlooped custom likelihood”. SDM uses loop = FALSE and no vars.
Add a model fitted to counts to uses_aggregate_data() in R/data_check.R (currently m3, ezdm and mpt), so that bmm_data_check() does not report too few observations per cell.

title: Appendix A — Reference
text:
A.5 Within-chain threading
You need this when your Stan code injects data or likelihood code through stanvar(), or your custom family uses vars with loop = FALSE.
Passing threads to bmm() asks brms to split each chain’s likelihood across cores. brms slices the response and calls the likelihood inside partial_log_lik, where the row bounds start and end exist. Two things it does not slice:

A custom family’s vars. brms pastes them in as written, so a vectorized likelihood would receive the whole vector next to a slice of the response. cswald therefore passes vars = "dec[start:end]" when threading and "dec" otherwise.
Stan code injected through stanvar(), which has to be written differently depending on whether it ends up inside partial_log_lik or in the model block.

Both decisions rest on brms_slices_likelihood() in R/utils.R. Call it in configure_model() rather than reading the brms.threads option yourself: it normalizes the option as brms does and is FALSE for threading(force = TRUE), where brms compiles with threading support but emits unsliced code. SDM, cswald and sdt_mafc use it.
SDM is the fullest example. inst/stan_chunks/ holds sdm_simple_likelihood.stan and sdm_simple_likelihood_threaded.stan, and configure_model.sdm() reads one of them:
likelihood_file <- if (brms_slices_likelihood()) {
  "sdm_simple_likelihood_threaded.stan"
} else {
  "sdm_simple_likelihood.stan"
}
Data the threaded likelihood needs must also be declared in the partial-log-likelihood signature through the pll_args argument of stanvar(). SDM passes "data matrix COSN" and, through its helper sdm_stanvar_int_array(), the run-index arrays. Without that, the variable is out of scope inside partial_log_lik and the model does not compile.
Test the generated Stan code with no threads, with threads = 2 and with threading(2, force = TRUE), as test-model_sdm-stancode.R does.

title: Appendix A — Reference
text:
A.6 Version tables
You need this when your model has several versions, or when you read an older model file and its structure differs from what the template generates.
use_model_template("mymodel", versions = c("v1", "v2")) generates a version table: the specification of each version in one lookup list, which the constructor indexes with version. EZDM, cswald and M3 use it:


R/model_ezdm.R

.ezdm_version_table <- list(
  "3par" = list(
    parameters = list(...),
    links = list(...),
    fixed_parameters = list(...),
    priors = list(...),
    init_ranges = list(...)
  ),
  "4par" = list(
    parameters = list(...),
    links = list(...),
    ...
  )
)

parameters = .ezdm_version_table[[version]][["parameters"]],
Keep the default of the alias’s version argument a literal c(...): model_versions() reads it to build the per-version documentation.
Two departures from this shape exist in the package:

M3 nests one level deeper. Its links and priors are indexed by the choice rule before the parameter (.m3_version_table[[version]][["links"]][[choice_rule]]), fixed_parameters is computed in the constructor, and the default version "custom" is not in the table at all, because the user supplies the specification. Copy this only if your model has a second axis of variation.
Some models write their specification inline. sdm, mixture2p, mixture3p, imm and most SDT models have no defaults list or version table, because they predate it. New models use the separated specification.

title: Appendix A — Reference
section: A.7 Choosing the sd prior rate
text:
A.7 Choosing the sd prior rate
You need this when you set the sd default priors of a new model.
The shipped models use exponential() on the link scale, with the rate chosen by what the parameter measures:







Rate
Parameters




1
sensitivity, memory strength, concentration (kappa), mixing weights, identity-linked drift


2
criteria and thresholds, boundary, non-decision time, start point, log-linked drift, diffusion constant, log ratios, log SDs, correlations


4
circular bias



The template repeats this table as a comment above the priors. Every model declares an sd prior, except the custom version of M3, which has no default priors at all.

title: Appendix A — Reference
text:
A.8 Naming traps
You need this when brms or Stan fails with an error that does not point at the cause, or when a parameter gets a prior you did not set.
A custom family’s dpars may not contain _ or ., and may not end with a digit. brms::custom_family() checks both, so neither delta_1 nor delta1 is a legal name. The digits on IMM parameters (kappa1, theta3) are generated by brms::mixture(), and parameters introduced through nlf() are not subject to this check.
Reusing a brms dpar name inherits its default prior. brms attaches default priors by name to mu, sigma, shape, nu, phi, kappa, beta, zi, hu, zoi, coi, bs, ndt, bias, quantile, xi, alpha, disc and theta, and strips trailing digits first, so kappa1 is treated as kappa. bmm reuses several of these names and sets its own defaults; the trap is a reused name you forget to give a default prior.
A dpar must not be uniquely prefixed by thres. brms reads p$thres when it builds a custom likelihood call, and $ partial-matches on lists, so a dpar named threshold is passed where ordinal thresholds belong. The result is Stan code that does not parse.
Stan probability-function suffixes need the bar syntax. A function whose name ends in _lpdf, _lupdf, _lpmf, _lupmf, _cdf, _lcdf or _lccdf must be called with a vertical bar between its first two arguments, as swald_lpdf(rt | drift, bound, ndt, s). If your helper is not really a distribution function, give it another name.
An nlf() right-hand side is pasted together as text, so operator precedence is yours to manage. The IMM parenthesizes every sub-expression it interpolates: "{lure_idx} * (-expS*{nt_distances} + c) + (1 - {lure_idx}) * (-100)".
Short parameter names collide. Besides the initial-value matching above (Section A.3), bmm treats a formula component as non-linear when one of its predictors is also a parameter. When the same name is also a data column, check_formula() warns, because the choice changes the likelihood without the user seeing it. One-letter parameters collide with columns such as a condition coded c.
